this amazake or amasake shop is located behind a small shrine, it is a 9 minute walk from Fushimi Inari Tiasha, aka the Senbon Torii (thousand torii gates). 

don’t ask me how I found it, it was very randomly on google 360 but the point being, this place is run by the lovely lady, Suzuki Kazuyote. her warmth and hospitality is unparalleled as you can already see in the video. 

both hot and cold amazake are available here and it is just for ¥500 which is absolutely insane. 

for those wondering, what is amazake? amazake is a traditional sweet low or non-alcoholic japanese drink made with fermented rice. essentially the alcohol percentage separates it from sake. 

if you are visiting senbon torii then you need to cool off here after the long hike (this too is about a 500 meter hike) but everything is worth the break from the tourists and having a traditional experience. it truly surprises me how lowkey this place is and it is barely on anyone’s radar.

caption:
There has never been a better time to buy a watch in Japan. 

1. Low Prices
Thanks to a number of macroeconomic factors that started in the ‘90s, the Japanese Yen is really low. The watch market has not fully adjusted yet so you are able to find amazing steals. On top of this, in Japan 10% VAT is deducted straight from the price at the shop.

2. Large Vintage Market
Due to its economic prosperity in the ‘80s, Tokyo is the best vintage city in the world. Particularly if you take into consideration Japan’s attitude towards good maintenance. You will be able to find rare and unique pieces in amazing condition.

3. Watch Trends
Japan doesn’t always follow the same trends as the rest of the world as it can be quite trend insular. Popular watches abroad are still unwanted here and priced accordingly.

Most importantly just enjoy your trip and lose yourself in the experience.

transcription: How safe is Tokyo's Red Light District? Let's talk about it. So Kabukucho, which is an area within Shinjuku, is widely considered to be Tokyo's Red Light District. It is a late night and adult entertainment hub. You will see a lot of raunchy advertisement when walking down some of these side streets and main street at night or in the evenings. You will encounter quite a few people that have had way too much to drink. And typically if you're a younger woman, you might also encounter some nampa. Nampa typically boils the men who try and pick up women, especially foreign women who might seem naive. They will keep trying to talk to you or try and talk to you in English in order to get you to go on a date with them or go to a hotel with them. Generally they're rather harmless but persistent. Now when it comes to actual safety in Kabukicho, what is it like? If you're just walking around and browsing casually, especially in a group, it's generally pretty okay. I'm used to areas like London and the Nightlife in London is far scarier than this. However, I do recommend being very careful when it comes to going to restaurants or bars in Kabukicho. For the love of God, do not follow a tout into any bar or restaurant. Don't go to anywhere that's being very pushy or is actively trying to promote it to English people. Because more often than not, they are running scams in order to get your card information or to overcharge you. And in some instances they will actually put something in your drink in order to steal your information and your items. So really drinking and eating in Kabukucho can be one of the biggest risks, especially as a tourist with no idea of the area. Although Kabukucho is relatively safe to walk around and explore even later nights, it is an area that is experiencing issues with trafficking, alcoholism, and of course he increased in Toyoko kids. So if you do plan to check out Kabukucho and I do think it's worth it, please just stay sensible and stay respectful.

#japan #tokyo #japanesefashion #japanesedenim #tokyofashion #japanmade #japanfashion #denim #baggyjeans #menes".
transcription: This is some of the rarest Japanese denim in Japan, because no craftsmen wanted to make it. Before being hand cut by experienced craftsmen in the capital of Japanese denim, it's passed through some of the last remaining vintage shuttles, but that's actually now what makes these so special because Japanese selvage denim comes from a more narrow fabric. It's actually too expensive to produce anything other than slim and straight fit jeans, but men's decided to change that by creating a completely different silhouette, meaning these are the only baggy fits selvage denim jeans that are actually produced in Japan. Other overseas brands label their baggy jeans as Japanese, but I haven't been able to find any actually made here in Japan. Completely removing all of the craftsmen's. On top of that, because Japanese denim is actually more durable, these baggie fit jeans hold their shape way better than other denim does. And despite the high cost production, men is actually selling theirs for less than other Japanese denim brands in order to keep the modern design accessible. The fact that they've managed to combine traditional Japanese craftsmanship with the modern design and keep it accessible is actually incredible. Okay, so I'm gonna nerd out here a little bit. Japanese denim is known for its indigo color. And I know that these are black, but in order to pay homage, they went with a Gilcret on their back of their pants, which is an indigo-colored flower. I thought it was a cool little subtle homage to the path.
